composition.assessment: Coherent connected narrative: two men have five animals; one requests help; the other agrees; the pair bind the animals; food is given to the companion; the final clause states the resulting condition.
form_checks: Twēgen męnn and fīf dēor match the already taught numeral/noun forms.
On ðǣm strande uses the already taught location frame and actual strand dative.
Se ǣresta mann and se ōðer mann preserve the earlier ordinal/other strong-weak scopes.
Helpe is present subjunctive second singular in a contextually tentative gif request; magon is ordinary present indicative capability.
Mē/ðē are dative helpan objects, not accusative by a default modern-English analogy.
Binden wē is first-plural exhortation; retaining n before wē is supported by Cook193a gān wē.
Bundon and sealde are earlier taught indicative past forms. His gefēran is the singular dative recipient, with actual prior gefera-dat-sg; męte is the food given.
Ðā dēor wǣron bunden has an explicitly allowed uninflected verbal predicate participle. It is not an attributive neuter-plural test.
scope_conditions: Teach the present tentative gif use before independent work.
Teach the selected bindan participle and verbal-passive rule before the reading.
Interpret personal references within the stated story rather than asserting that every possessive/pronoun has a uniquely forced antecedent in isolation.

teaching_examples.note: Statement versus third-plural wish; masculine sǣ dative matches the active selection.
Gāð is second-plural imperative; gān wē is first-plural subjunctive exhortation, directly paralleled by Cook193a.
Capability, permission and wish are distinct; no automatic equivalence of English may and subjunctive.
Open gif condition has ordinary indicatives and a dative recipient of food; gif itself does not impose subjunctive.
Tentative help request requires the stated context; present subjunctive condition plus indicative main capability is grammatical.

Cōme/hulpe are complete lexical preterite-subjunctive cells. Nonpast unreal setting and interpretation must be supplied. This is a new illustration, not a source quotation or general autonomous counterfactual template.
Bindenda is masculine nominative singular weak attributive participle after se; do not confuse with an -end agent noun.

Both uninflected bunden and masculine-like plural bundene are permitted in a verbal predicate by Cook62/179. The selected attributive strong-neuter-plural model has bundenu with accepted variants bundene and bunden, so the surface spellings overlap. The distinction is syntactic: attributive forms receive gender/case/number agreement analysis; predicates permit uninflection or masculine-like endings. Do not invent an exclusive spelling contrast or reject the listed attributive variants.
An accusative bound animal becomes the nominative passive subject, with past event auxiliary wearð. The elementary rule applies to this taught accusative frame.
Bēo is an imperative in an explicitly second-singular command; bēon is third-plural subjunctive with the birds. The spellings alone do not eliminate formal homography.

Hātan naming has two accusatives; Heofon is an editorial capitalized name, based on the ordinary heofon accusative stem. Tō tācne is the selected dative function phrase, not an infinitival purpose construction.
